introduction-the-tower-of-babel.core: Modern stacks mix Go, Python, Java and Rust. They need a shared language: a schema over the network (Protobuf/gRPC) or a C ABI inside one process (FFI).

first_principles.problem: Services in different languages miscommunicate: field names drift, types don't match and hand-written clients break.
truths: Each language has its own native types.
Network calls and in-process calls have different costs.
derivation: Inside one process: the **C ABI** through FFI.

analogy.title: A multilingual kitchen
analogy.story: French, Italian and Mandarin-speaking chefs share standard order tickets so every dish comes out right.
analogy.breaks: Contracts must evolve carefully, or one chef misreads an updated ticket.

example.title: A Go API with a Python ML model
flow: Option B: Python calls Rust lib via FFI (in-process)

check.q: What are the two main interop approaches?
check.a: Network serialisation with a schema (Protobuf/gRPC) and in-process FFI via the C ABI.

protocol-buffers-protobuf-the-universal-.core: Protobuf defines messages in a .proto schema and generates typed code for every language. It encodes compact binary with numbered fields, so it's smaller and faster than JSON and evolves safely.

first_principles.problem: JSON repeats field names in every message, has loose types and gives no schema-enforced contract between teams.
derivation: **Never reuse field numbers**; add new fields to evolve.

analogy.title: A pre-printed form with numbered boxes
analogy.story: Everyone knows box 3 means 'quantity', so you write only the values, never the labels.
analogy.breaks: Binary isn't human-readable, so debugging needs tools like grpcurl or protoc --decode.

example.title: A user message

steps.label: Evolve
steps.detail: Add `string team = 4;` and old clients simply ignore it.

example.outcome: fast, typed and evolvable cross-language data.

check.q: Why must you never reuse a field number?
check.a: Old data or clients would interpret the new field's bytes as the old field, corrupting meaning.

foreign-function-interfaces-ffi-crossing.core: FFI lets one language call functions compiled in another (usually through the C ABI) inside the same process, with no serialisation or network. It's ideal for hot paths like calling a Rust library from Python.

first_principles.problem: Even fast gRPC adds microseconds to milliseconds per call, which is too slow for millions of tight calls.
truths: Network calls need serialisation and kernel transitions.
Functions in one process call each other in nanoseconds.
The C ABI is the common denominator.
derivation: Compile the library with a **C-compatible ABI** (extern "C").
Load it from the host (ctypes, cffi, PyO3, cgo, JNI).

analogy.title: Talking face to face vs. by post
analogy.story: Post (network) needs envelopes and delivery time; face to face (FFI) is instant but requires being in the same room.
analogy.breaks: Being in the same room means sharing risks too: a crash in the library kills the host.

example.title: Python calling a Rust hashing library

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Native speed with no network hop.

check.q: When is FFI preferable to gRPC?
check.a: For very frequent, latency-critical calls where serialisation and network overhead dominate.

ffi-risks-here-be-dragons.core: FFI drops the host language's safety net: memory leaks, buffer overflows and segfaults in native code crash the whole process, and ownership and threading rules must be handled by hand at the boundary.

first_principles.problem: A small bug in a C extension segfaults a Python service with no traceback.
truths: Native code has no GC or bounds checks.
Both sides must agree who frees memory.
Crashes cross the boundary as process death.
derivation: Define **memory ownership** explicitly (who allocates, who frees).
**Isolate risky code** in a subprocess when stability matters.

analogy.title: Leaving the climbing gym for a real cliff
analogy.story: Indoors there are mats and auto-belays; outside, a slip is a real fall.
analogy.breaks: Memory-safe native languages such as Rust with PyO3 reduce, but don't remove, these risks.

example.title: A leaky string return
flow: Fix: export free_string() and call it

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Every boundary needs an explicit ownership contract.

example.outcome: FFI is used with deliberate safety rules.

check.q: Why can FFI bugs be worse than normal bugs?
check.a: Native crashes and memory corruption take down the whole host process with no exception to catch.
